note_claims.claim: The patient presented with a first seizure 3 weeks ago.
The seizure involved the patient going quiet, followed by left arm jerking for a few seconds, generalized stiffening, and shaking lasting about 5 minutes.
The patient experienced perioral cyanosis, lateral tongue bite, and urinary incontinence during the seizure.
The patient was confused for about 20 minutes post-seizure.
The seizure was preceded by sleep deprivation due to four consecutive night shifts.
The patient reported no alcohol consumption that day, only having a few pints at the weekend.
The patient reported no recreational drug use.
The patient has no history of previous seizures, myoclonic jerks, or absences.
The patient has no history of head injury or CNS infection.
The patient has no family history of epilepsy.
The neurological examination was completely normal.
The CT scan in A&E and blood tests were normal.
The presentation is a first generalized tonic-clonic seizure, possibly of focal onset (left arm, suggesting right hemisphere), provoked in part by sleep deprivation.
No antiseizure medication is required at present.
An MRI scan of the brain using an epilepsy protocol and an EEG are planned.
The patient must not drive and must inform the DVLA (usually 6 months off driving after a first seizure).
If a further seizure occurs, the patient should put him in the recovery position, time it, and call 999 if it lasts more than five minutes or if he is injured.

transcript_facts.fact: Clinician is Dr Iyer from the first seizure clinic.
Relative is Bethany, the patient's wife.
Patient recalls watching telly and then paramedics arrived in the living room.
The event occurred three weeks ago on a Sunday night.
Relative describes the event: the patient went quiet, then his left arm started jerking for a few seconds, followed by generalized stiffening and shaking all over.
Relative states the shaking felt like five minutes, but when checking the clock, it lasted two minutes.
Relative describes symptoms: his lips went a bit blue, he bit his tongue on the side, and he wet himself.
Relative states the patient was really confused for about twenty minutes afterwards.
Patient history: He has done four night shifts in a row and had maybe four hours' sleep.
Patient history: He has no alcohol that day, only having a few pints at the weekend.
Patient history: He has no recreational drug use.
Patient history: He has never had anything like this before, including funny turns, jerks in the morning, or blank spells.
Patient history: He has no history of head injuries or meningitis as a child.
Patient history: He has no family history of epilepsy.
Patient history: He has no regular medications and no known drug allergies.
Patient history: He drives to work.
Examination finding: Neurological examination is completely normal today.
Examination finding: CT scan in A&E was normal.
Examination finding: Blood tests were normal.
Clinician's impression: This sounds like a seizure, possibly of focal onset (left arm, suggesting right hemisphere), provoked in part by lack of sleep.
Plan: The clinician recommends an MRI scan of the brain using an epilepsy protocol and an EEG.
Plan: No antiseizure medication is usually needed after a first seizure; decisions will be made after results.
Plan: The patient must not drive and needs to inform the DVLA (usually 6 months off driving after a first seizure).
Plan: The patient's employer may be able to help with shifts, and he should not drive in the meantime.
Safety tips: have showers, not baths; don't swim alone; avoid heights; try to keep a regular sleep pattern.
Safety-netting: If a further seizure happens, put him on his side, time it, and call 999 if it lasts more than five minutes or he is injured.
Follow-up: The patient will see the clinician in about six weeks with the results.

findings.transcript_evidence: It felt like five minutes. But I looked at the clock when it started and when it stopped, and it was two minutes.
findings.rationale: The note inaccurately records the duration of the seizure, which is contradicted by the transcript evidence.
